name: Neurodiversity
summary: Neurodiversity is the view that variation in human neurocognitive functioning, autism and ADHD included, is a natural and valuable form of human diversity rather than a set of disorders. Its paradigm holds that the idea of one normal brain is a cultural fiction, and that the disadvantages neurodivergent people face are largely produced by social barriers and prejudice. Its movement seeks civil rights, respect and inclusion, opposes attempts to eliminate autism, and wants neurodivergent people to take part in every decision about them. Its sources say little about economics, government or foreign affairs.
scope: The neurodiversity paradigm and movement as defined by Nick Walker's 'Neurodiversity: Some Basic Terms & Definitions' and Judy Singer's own definition, and as described in the scholarly review by Pellicano and den Houting (2022). It covers the paradigm's three principles and the movement's civil-rights aims for neurominorities. It leaves out the biological fact of neurodiversity itself (which Walker and Singer say is not a position), the wider social model of disability and the disability rights movement, and any single organisation's positions beyond what the sources present as the movement's own.

aliases.name: neurodiversity movement
aliases.quote: The Neurodiversity Movement is a social justice movement that seeks civil rights, equality, respect, and full societal inclusion for the neurodivergent.

aliases.name: neurodiversity paradigm
aliases.quote: The neurodiversity paradigm thus promotes autism acceptance

furtherReading.title: Neurodiversity: Some Basic Terms & Definitions (Nick Walker)
furtherReading.note: The most cited short statement of the paradigm's three principles and the movement's aims.

furtherReading.title: Neurodiversity: Definition and Discussion (Judy Singer)
furtherReading.note: The term's coiner on what she meant by it and how it connects to civil rights and intersectionality.

furtherReading.title: Shifting from 'normal science' to neurodiversity in autism science (Pellicano and den Houting)
furtherReading.note: An open-access scholarly review of the paradigm's history and core tenets.

furtherReading.title: What We Believe (Autistic Self Advocacy Network)
furtherReading.note: A plain-language account of the movement's views on school, work, health care and research.

keyFigures.name: Judy Singer
keyFigures.role: Australian sociologist who coined the word 'neurodiversity' in her 1998 thesis

keyFigures.name: Nick Walker
keyFigures.role: Scholar who set out the paradigm's basic terms and principles in 2014

sources.title: Neurodiversity: Some Basic Terms & Definitions
sources.author: Nick Walker
sources.usedFor: The paradigm's three principles, the movement's aims and the line between neurodiversity, the paradigm and the movement.

sources.title: Neurodiversity: Definition and Discussion
sources.author: Judy Singer

missingStatements.text: Autism should not be treated as something to cure.
missingStatements.rationale: The movement opposes attempts to get rid of autism and similar innate neurodivergences, treating them as part of who a person is.

quotes.text: The neurodiversity paradigm rejects the pathologizing of such forms of neurodivergence, and the Neurodiversity Movement opposes attempts to get rid of them.
The neurodiversity movement also says that we shouldn’t try to cure or get rid of autism.
quotes.where: Neurodiversity and Disability Rights, What is Neurodiversity?

missingStatements.text: Disabled people should have a say in every decision that affects them.
missingStatements.rationale: The paradigm stresses self-determination: affected people take part in every decision about them, from policy to individual support.

quotes.text: autistic people must be involved in all decision‐making that stands to affect autistic people, from the highest levels of policy development to individual support planning
“Nothing About Us Without Us” means that autistic people need to be involved whenever autism is discussed.

notes: Themes searched: the definitions (Walker, Singer), the scholarly review (Pellicano and den Houting), ASAN's statement of belief for school, work, health care, research and cure. They state positions on disability, medicine and discrimination, and nearly none on economy, government, world affairs, technology or ecology. Organisational positions of ASAN on health care funding, welfare or policing are one organisation's and are not used. Singer's critique of 'economic rationalism' is not a position on capitalism or markets. Walker allows consensual cure of epilepsy-type conditions but not of autism; Singer says she critiques both the medical and social models, so no answer rests on the social model.
